name: Google
summary: A structured panel of interviews scored against shared rubrics. Software roles lean on coding, with design for experienced hires.

sources.title: Ten things we know to be true

process.note: Google says the steps and timeline vary by role, and that AI tools are not allowed during interviews. Round counts and lengths below are what candidates commonly report, not official figures.

stages.name: Assessments
stages.detail: Some roles start with an online hiring assessment about workstyle, and sometimes a role-related exercise such as a coding test.

stages.name: Recruiter calls
stages.detail: Usually one or two short phone or video calls about the role, key skills and the timeline.

stages.name: Interview panel
stages.detail: A panel of interviews over video or in person. Every candidate for a role is scored on the same structured rubric. Candidates often report about 45 minutes per round.

stages.name: Review
stages.detail: Your application and all interview feedback are reviewed together before a decision.

design.note: Design rounds are commonly reported for experienced roles. Expect to reason about scale, storage and trade-offs out loud.

values.title: What Google says it looks for
values.summary: Google's interview tips ask you to draw on past work, show how you handle ambiguity, and explain how you work with and lead others. Its philosophy page puts the user first.

items.name: Learn from past work
items.gist: Bring concrete examples from earlier projects and what they taught you.

items.name: Handle ambiguity
items.gist: Ask clarifying questions and show how you make progress when the problem is fuzzy.

items.name: Work with people
items.gist: Show how you collaborate, disagree well and help a team succeed.

items.name: Lead without the title
items.gist: Describe times you rallied others through communication and good decisions.

items.name: Focus on the user
items.gist: Tie your choices back to the people who use what you build.

prompts.text: Describe a project where the goal was unclear at the start. How did you find a direction?
Tell a story where you got a group moving without being the official lead.
Talk about a decision where you put the user ahead of an easier engineering path.
Share a piece of work that did not go to plan and what you changed afterwards.

mock.note: Follows the interview panel: two coding rounds, a design round for experienced roles and a leadership and teamwork conversation.
